newsitem.title: VATICAN: Netanyahu invites Pope, firm on Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu invites Pope, firm on Jerusalem.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday invited Pope John Paul to visit the Holy Land and said such a historic trip would help cement peace between Jews and Arabs.

The Israeli leader said he had also told the Pontiff at their Vatican audience that he was adamant that Jerusalem, a city sacred to Moslems, Christians and Jews, should remain Israel's "united and eternal capital".
The Vatican, which like most other countries keeps its embassy in or near Tel Aviv, wants international guarantees protecting Jerusalem as sacred for Christians, Moslems and Jews.
Netanyahu, on his way home from talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, was visiting Rome for the first time since his election last May.
"We look forward to receiving you in Jerusalem," Netanyahu said as he left the Roman Catholic Pontiff's study after a 20-minute private audience at the Vatican.
The Polish Pope responded: "God Bless Israel".
No date for an eventual visit was given but Netanyahu said the Pope had told him that he hoped to make the trip before 2000, the start of Christianity's third millennium.

"I think that he (the Pope) would be welcomed by thousands and thousands of young people, by Jews and Arabs alike in the same place," Netanyahu told a news conference after meeting Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
"It would be a great message of hope for the Middle East and also for our peace with our neighbours," he said.
A trip to the Holy Land, one of the 76-year-old Pope's cherished dreams, would be the first by a Roman Catholic leader since Paul VI visited in 1964.

The Pope last year accepted an invitation by Arafat to visit Christ's birthplace in Bethlehem at the turn of the millennium and has a standing invitation from Israel last made in 1994 by the late prime minister Yitzhak Rabin.

A Vatican statement on the audience said the Pope told Netanyahu he hoped Jerusalem could be a place where "Jews, Christians, Moslems, Israelis and Arabs, believers and non-believers can create and consolidate a concrete peace in respect of everyone's rights and dignity".
Netanyahu said he had explained Israel's commitment to the free worship of all three faiths in the city but also " very clearly that we want to keep Jerusalem a united city".

"We don't want to re-divide the city, we don't want to rebuild a Berlin Wall in the centre of the city because at the end of the day this would not only go against our interests for Jerusalem as the eternal capital of the Jewish people.
"It would go against the universality of Jerusalem as the centre of worship of the three great faiths," Netanyahu said.

Palestinians view East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in the 1967 Six-Day War, as the capital of a future state. Arafat said during a visit to Rome last year that Jerusalem would either make or break Middle East peace.
The Vatican and Israel ended nearly 2,000 years of often hostile Catholic-Jewish relations in 1994 when they established full diplomatic relations.
The two sides have since been working towards agreement on issues regarding the legal status of the Catholic Church and its clerical hierarchy in the Jewish state.
Netanyahu said relations had "never been better and they will get even better".
